extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, in-house counsel, IP professionals, and companies evaluating patent risk or drafting method claims
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of how the Federal Circuit's Akamai and McKesson decisions affect inducement liability in divided infringement scenarios and implications for claim drafting, enforcement, and freedom-to-operate assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divided infringement definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenarios where a single entity does not perform every element of a claim, but different entities perform different steps of a claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include customers performing critical steps (e.g., a doctor performing a collection or diagnostic step, or a server user modifying a webpage). The concept is especially relevant as end-user sophistication and web/mobile/cloud technologies increase the likelihood of multi-actor performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability primarily to method claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The divided infringement issue essentially only occurs in method claims where it is often advantageous to divide the steps of a task among different entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For non-method claims, the entity that installs the final part typically completes the claimed invention, so induced infringement without a direct infringer is generally not possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement (§271(a)) single-entity rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Under §271(a) (make, use, or sell), divided infringement is a complete defense because direct infringement follows the single-entity rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited precedent: Warner-Jenkinson Corp. v. Hilton Davis Corp. Infringement under §271(a) is treated as strict liability (intent irrelevant except for damages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inducement (§271(b)) can apply without a single direct infringer (Akamai/McKesson ruling)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit held that inducement under §271(b) does not require a single, direct infringer — knowingly inducing performance of each claim limitation, regardless of who performs it, can constitute inducement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per the combined en banc decision (Akamai Tech. v. Limelight Networks and McKesson Tech. v. Epic Systems), entities cannot be immunized merely because they delegated steps to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two divided-infringement scenarios addressed
rubrics_metrics.description: 1) A defendant performs some steps and induces others to perform remaining steps. 2) A defendant induces multiple parties to collectively perform all steps, but no single party performs every step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both scenarios were presented to and considered by the court and inform how inducement may be applied in multi-actor situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent/knowledge requirement for inducement
rubrics_metrics.description: The first prong of the inducement test requires that a joint infringer knowingly induce the activity; inducement under §271(b) is not strict liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The intent prong likely requires knowledge of the asserted patent and knowledge that the induced (and divided) activities collectively infringe the asserted patent. This mental-state requirement narrows liability to knowing/nefarious actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast between §271(a) strict liability and §271(b) intent requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement under §271(a) is strict liability (intent irrelevant except for damages), whereas §271(b) inducement requires intent and is not strict liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authority: In re Seagate Tech.; the distinction affects plaintiffs' burdens and potential remedies in divided infringement cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedent overruled (BMC and Muniauction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit overruled earlier Federal Circuit precedent (BMC Resources v. Paymentech and Muniauction v. Thomson) that had imposed a single-entity requirement for inducement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should note that prior case law that protected defendants based on lack of a single direct infringer has been narrowed/abrogated by the en banc decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft method claims to be performed by a single infringer (best practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, draft method claims such that a single infringer would practice every claim step so that direct infringement under §271(a) (strict liability) applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice avoids reliance on inducement theories (which require intent) and preserves more settled paths to damages and injunctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use transformative treatment step to capture divided actors and avoid §101 risk
rubrics_metrics.description: In some cases (e.g., personalized medicine diagnostics involving data gathering, analysis, correlation, and treatment by different entities), adding a transformative treatment step may allow claims performed by divided entities to avoid dismissal under §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This technique can enable protection of previously unpatentable or narrowly-drafted claims by ensuring the claim recites a transformative act, but must be balanced against claim breadth and validity risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revisit freedom-to-operate (FTO) and competitor claim analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies should revisit prior FTO analyses where non-infringement conclusions were based on the absence of a single party performing every step of a claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-Akamai/McKesson, inducement theories may expose risk even when no single actor performed all claim steps; counsel should re-evaluate infringement risk accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncertainties remain regarding remedies (damages/injunction) in divided infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The majority did not fully address how damages or the ability to obtain an injunction operate under divided infringement scenarios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should be cautious: even if liability can be established via inducement, practical remedies and enforcement mechanisms may be unsettled and could be challenged on appeal or by the Supreme Court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industries most affected
rubrics_metrics.description: Software, business methods, diagnostics, and biotechnology are particularly impacted due to common use of method claims and multi-actor implementations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As cloud/mobile/web technologies and personalized medicine grow, the likelihood of divided-infringement scenarios increases; practitioners in these fields should pay special attention to claim drafting and enforcement strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy and dissent perspectives (cautionary context)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dissenting judges argued that patentees can usually draft claims to capture a single-party infringer and that expanding inducement liability is a judicial creation with uncertain policy consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awareness of dissenting views is important because they reflect potential avenues for future legal challenge and underscore that the decision is contentious and may be narrowed or reversed.
